sections.explanation: An identity is true for every permitted input, for example 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6. An equation asks which inputs make a statement true, for example 2x + 3 = 7. A numerical coincidence is agreement at a particular input without general equivalence. The domain matters: x/x = 1 is an identity only for x ≠ 0. One permitted counterexample disproves a universal claim; many agreeing examples do not prove it.
sections.worked: x² = x is true at x = 0 and x = 1, but false at x = 2 because 4 ≠ 2. Two successful tests did not establish an identity. By contrast, distributing 3(x − 2) gives 3x − 6 for all real x.

sections.explanation: To establish an identity, transform one side using valid algebraic laws until it matches the other, retaining restrictions. Avoid assuming the equality you are trying to establish. To reject a proposed identity, show one permitted input with unequal results. Choose inputs strategically: zero may erase the very terms that differ, so a non-zero value can be more informative.
sections.worked: Claim: 2(x − 3) + x = 3x − 6. Expanding the left gives 2x − 6 + x = 3x − 6, proving it. Claim: (x + 2)² = x² + 4. At x = 1, 9 ≠ 5, disproving it.

sections.explanation: Use code to explore a claim, while keeping the distinction between testing and proof explicit. Assign one input at a time and evaluate both expressions. The comparison == returns a Boolean. Here use small integers so arithmetic is exact. Floating-point equality is not a general test of numerical accuracy; we will return to that limitation later. Do not introduce a loop yet: make each chosen example intentional.
sections.worked: The code tests the false claim x² = x at x = 2. It prints 4, 2 and False. Reassigning x = 1 and rerunning makes the comparison True without changing the status of the universal claim.

sections.explanation: Retrieve the ideas without looking back first. A complete answer should state the claim, domain, method and conclusion. If you miss a task, identify whether the issue is distribution, cancellation, restriction, code syntax or the logic of evidence. Return to that specific lesson and attempt a fresh example. This is practice for a checkable mathematical argument, not a requirement to work quickly.
sections.worked: For (x² − x)/x = x − 1, write x ≠ 0 first, factor x(x − 1), and cancel. A numerical check at x = 3 yields 2 in both forms. The factorisation establishes equivalence on the domain.
